title: Math & Number Theory for Interviews
summary: A pocket toolbox — gcd, primes, modular arithmetic, fast power — that turns "impossible" interview constraints into clean, overflow-safe code.

blocks.markdown:
Four small tricks cover almost every "math-y" interview problem.

- **gcd / lcm** via the Euclidean algorithm — sync cycles, reduce fractions.
- **Primes** — trial-divide one number to √N; sieve to list all up to N.
- **Modular arithmetic** — "clock math" that keeps huge counts from overflowing.
- **Fast exponentiation** — `a^n` in O(log n) by squaring, not O(n).

Everything else here is built from these four.

blocks.subTitle: Which tool when
blocks.markdown:
Match the constraint to the tool before you write a line.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Reduce a fraction / sync two cycles | gcd / lcm |
| "Is N prime?" once | trial division to √N |
| "All primes up to N" | Sieve of Eratosthenes |
| `a^n mod m`, big n | binary exponentiation |
| Divide under a prime mod | modular inverse (Fermat) |

blocks.subTitle: gcd & lcm via Euclid
blocks.markdown:
Any divisor of `a` and `b` also divides `a mod b`, so `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)`.

```python
def gcd(a, b):
    while b:
        a, b = b, a % b
    return a

def lcm(a, b):
    return a // gcd(a, b) * b   # divide first, avoid overflow
```

- Replace the pair with **(b, remainder)** until the remainder is 0.
- Time **O(log min(a,b))** — the remainder shrinks exponentially.
- `lcm` divides *before* multiplying so the middle value stays small.

blocks.subTitle: Primes & the sieve
blocks.markdown:
To test one N, trial-divide up to **√N** — a larger factor always pairs with a smaller one. To list every prime up to N, cross out multiples.

![Sieve of Eratosthenes crossing out multiples up to 30](assets/a19-math-number-theory/sieve-of-eratosthenes.svg)

- Start all numbers "prime"; for each prime p, cross out **p², p²+p, …**.
- Stop once **p > √N** — every composite already has a smaller factor.
- Sieve is **O(N log log N)** time, **O(N)** space.

assets.alt: Sieve of Eratosthenes crossing out multiples up to 30

blocks.subTitle: Modular arithmetic
blocks.markdown:
Working "mod m" keeps only the remainder — like a clock wrapping past 12.

- **+, −, ×** all distribute: `(a × b) mod m = ((a mod m) × (b mod m)) mod m`.
- So take the mod at *every* step; the final answer is identical but values stay tiny.
- After subtraction, normalize: `((x mod m) + m) mod m` to avoid negatives.
- **Division does not distribute** — that needs a modular inverse.

blocks.subTitle: Why mod 1e9+7
blocks.markdown:
Counting problems say "return the answer mod 1e9+7" so the result never overflows.

- **1e9+7 is prime** — which makes modular inverse easy via Fermat.
- It sits just under 2³⁰, so one value fits in 32 bits.
- Two such values multiplied stay under ~10¹⁸ — safe in a signed **64-bit** int.
- `998244353` is the other common modulus (used for number-theoretic transforms).

blocks.subTitle: Fast exponentiation
blocks.markdown:
Write `n` in binary; `a^n` is the product of the squares `a, a², a⁴, …` whose bit is set.

![Fast exponentiation of 3 to the 13th by repeated squaring](assets/a19-math-number-theory/fast-exponentiation.svg)

- `3^13` (13 = 1101): multiply in 3⁸·3⁴·3¹ — **4 multiplies, not 12**.
- Each loop strips one bit of `n`, so it runs in **O(log n)**.
- Square the base every step; multiply into the result only on a set bit.

assets.alt: Fast exponentiation of 3 to the 13th by repeated squaring

blocks.subTitle: Modular inverse & combinatorics
blocks.markdown:
You can't divide under a mod — multiply by the **inverse**: `(a/b) mod m = a · b⁻¹ mod m`. When m is prime, Fermat gives a one-liner.

```python
def mod_inverse(b, m):   # m must be prime
    return pow(b, m - 2, m)
```

- This unlocks `C(n,k) mod p` despite its division.
- **Pascal's triangle** is division-free: `C(n,k) = C(n−1,k−1) + C(n−1,k)`.
- Permutations `P(n,k)=n!/(n−k)!`; combinations `C(n,k)=n!/(k!(n−k)!)`.

blocks.subTitle: Trial division vs sieve
blocks.markdown:
Both find primes — pick by how many you need.

| Aspect | Trial division | Sieve |
|---|---|---|
| Per query | O(√N) | O(1) after build |
| Memory | O(1) | O(N) |
| Best for | a few numbers | many / repeated |

The sieve can't run when N ≈ 10¹² — you can't allocate a trillion booleans. Then trial-divide individuals.

blocks.subTitle: Pascal vs factorials+inverse
blocks.markdown:
Two ways to compute combinations under a mod.

- **Pascal's triangle** — dead simple, division-free, but **O(N²)** time and space; caps near N ≈ a few thousand.
- **Factorials + Fermat inverse** — **O(N)** setup, **O(1)** per query, scales to N ≈ 10⁶, but needs a prime modulus.
- Small N and zero division bugs → Pascal. Large N → precompute factorials.

blocks.subTitle: Where this math lives
blocks.markdown:
These tools run real systems, not just contests.

- **RSA** — keygen multiplies large primes; encrypt/decrypt is modular exponentiation (the fast-power loop).
- **Hashing** — `value mod tableSize`, often a prime size to spread keys ([a03-hashing](a03-hashing.md)).
- **Rabin–Karp** — a rolling hash mod a large prime, updated O(1) per shift ([a10-tries-string-algorithms](a10-tries-string-algorithms.md)).
- **Checksums / sharding** — modular-polynomial CRCs and key→node mapping.

blocks.subTitle: Interview patterns
blocks.markdown:
Map the prompt to the tool fast.

- **Pow(x, n)** → binary exponentiation; guard `n = INT_MIN`.
- **Count Primes** → sieve, then count survivors.
- **Unique Paths** → it's just `C(m+n−2, m−1)`.
- **"… mod 1e9+7"** → counting DP, mod after every addition ([a14-dynamic-programming-1](a14-dynamic-programming-1.md)).
- **"When do cycles of a and b coincide?"** → `lcm(a, b)`.

The mistakes that fail the big test cases:

- **"Mod at the end."** Too late — it already overflowed. Mod after *every* multiply.
- **Negative mod.** `(-3) % 7` is often `-3`; normalize with `((x % m) + m) % m`.
- **lcm overflow.** Divide before multiply: `a / gcd * b`, never `a * b / gcd`.
- **Dividing under a mod.** No distributive law — use the modular inverse.
- **Fermat misuse.** Needs m prime and a not a multiple of m, else extended Euclid.
- **0 and 1 aren't prime.** Set `isPrime[0]=isPrime[1]=false`.
